entries.claim: An AI agent hacked into a crypto wallet and stole funds — AI systems are dangerous, uncontrollable financial threats
entries.verdict_summary: The incident reflects a targeted prompt-injection attack on a specific experimental system, not evidence that AI agents are broadly unsafe or uncontrollable.
entries.what_is_true: The concern here is legitimate at its core: AI agents with autonomous tool access — including the ability to sign transactions or move funds — represent a genuinely novel attack surface. When an AI agent can take real-world financial actions, a successful manipulation of that agent has real financial consequences. The OpenAI-reported incident, in which an AI agent was manipulated via prompt injection to exfiltrate cryptocurrency, is a real event and not something to wave away.
entries.what_data_shows: What the incident actually demonstrates is a known, documented class of vulnerability — prompt injection — being successfully exploited against a specific experimental deployment, not a flaw in AI reasoning or alignment broadly. Prompt injection attacks are an active research area with published mitigations. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications has listed prompt injection as the primary risk since 2023, and the security community has been building defenses including input sandboxing, privilege separation, and confirmation gates for agentic systems. The agent involved was not a production consumer product — it was operating in a context that granted it wallet access without the layered authorization controls that responsible deployment frameworks require. Framing this as 'AI stole money' obscures that the failure mode is architectural, not intrinsic to AI.
entries.bigger_picture: The history of every transformative financial technology — online banking, APIs, mobile payments — includes early-stage exploits that drove the development of robust security standards. The correct read on this incident is that the agentic AI ecosystem is moving through exactly that maturation process, and fast. OpenAI publicly disclosed the incident, the security research community has the receipts, and enterprise deployments are already implementing human-in-the-loop approval requirements for financial actions. Incidents like this harden the ecosystem. They do not prove the technology is irredeemably broken.

entries.what_is_true: The numbers deserve to be taken seriously. If $137 million was spent on AI-generated political advertising ahead of the midterms and only 27% of those ads carried a disclosure identifying AI involvement, that is a meaningful transparency failure. Voters have a legitimate interest in knowing when the images, voices, or video in a political ad were synthetically generated. Google banned AI-generated content in election ads that it cannot verify as authentic in November 2023. Meta requires disclosure labels on AI-generated political content. YouTube has required disclosure of realistic synthetic media in political ads since 2024. The genuine problem — that enforcement lags the technology — is real but is a governance challenge, not evidence that AI has made political deception unstoppable. The tools to detect, label, and enforce already exist. The story here is about political will, not technological inevitability.

Banks initially refused to integrate with Plaid, Venmo, and open banking APIs for the same regulatory and liability reasons — and then built the frameworks that made those integrations safe and ubiquitous. The same process is underway with agentic AI. The OCC, CFPB, and FDIC are all actively developing guidance on AI agents in financial services. It ignores that open-source AI models like Llama and Mistral are distributing capability outside corporate walls. It ignores that AI is compressing the cost of starting businesses, creating more entrepreneurs and more competition, not less. The legitimate policy debates — around antitrust, AI taxation, universal basic income pilots, and worker retraining investment — are important precisely because they can shape the distribution of AI's gains. entries.claim: Bitcoin is toast — quantum computers are going to break its encryption and there's no plan to stop it
entries.verdict_summary: The quantum threat to Bitcoin's cryptography is real in theory but decades away in practice, and post-quantum migration is already underway with clear technical pathways.
entries.what_is_true: The underlying cryptographic concern is legitimate. Bitcoin's ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) signature scheme is theoretically vulnerable to a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm. NIST and the broader cryptographic community have been explicit: if a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) were built, it could eventually compromise public-key cryptography used not just by Bitcoin but by TLS, SSH, and essentially all modern secure communications. This is not science fiction — it is the reason NIST spent six years running a post-quantum cryptography standardization process that concluded in 2024.
entries.what_data_shows: The key word is 'eventually.' Current quantum computers — including IBM's 1,121-qubit Condor and Google's Willow chip — operate with error rates that require millions of physical qubits to produce the thousands of stable logical qubits needed to run Shor's algorithm against a 256-bit elliptic curve key. Most peer-reviewed estimates, including from the Global Risk Institute's 2024 quantum threat timeline report, place a CRQC capable of breaking Bitcoin's encryption at 10 to 15 years away at minimum, with many placing it further. Coinbase's published quantum preparedness framework specifically proposes transitioning Bitcoin to NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms (CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium) — the same standards NIST finalized in August 2024. The technical migration path exists and is being actively designed.
entries.bigger_picture: The internet's entire security infrastructure faces the same quantum migration challenge as Bitcoin, and the response is the same: proactive algorithm replacement well ahead of the threat horizon. NIST's finalized post-quantum standards give developers, including Bitcoin Core contributors, concrete targets to migrate to. The fact that Coinbase is publishing a quantum preparedness roadmap now — while threat timelines remain a decade out — is the system working correctly. Framing this as 'Bitcoin is toast' ignores that every major cryptographic transition in internet history, from MD5 to SHA-256, from RSA-1024 to RSA-2048, has been executed successfully before the deprecation became a crisis.

entries.claim: Bitcoin is doomed — quantum computers will crack its encryption and steal every wallet

NIST finalized its first post-quantum cryptographic standards in August 2024 (FIPS 203, 204, 205), and Coinbase's own proposal outlines a concrete migration path for Bitcoin's protocol.
entries.bigger_picture: The quantum threat to Bitcoin is real in the same way that climate projections for 2075 are real — serious enough to plan for now, not a present emergency. The cryptography community identified this threat years before quantum hardware could plausibly execute it, which is exactly how responsible preparedness works. Post-quantum migration in Bitcoin is technically achievable through a soft or hard fork, and the conversation Coinbase is forcing is the right one to have in 2025. The headline 'Bitcoin is doomed' misreads a proactive risk management discussion as a death sentence. The encryption will be upgraded long before the threat is executable.

entries.claim: AI is destroying Wikipedia — the community that survived everything finally got killed by ChatGPT
entries.verdict_summary: Wikipedia's editor community is adapting to AI, not collapsing — active editor counts have stabilized and AI is increasingly used as a productivity tool by volunteers, not a replacement for them.
entries.what_is_true: Wikipedia has faced a genuine long-term editor decline since 2007, and the rise of AI chatbots has measurably reduced direct traffic to Wikipedia pages as users get answers without clicking through. These are real, documented trends. The Wikimedia Foundation's own traffic data confirms referral losses from search-integrated AI features. It is also true that some Wikipedians initially dismissed AI as a fad and have had to reckon with being wrong about the pace of change. That intellectual humility deserves acknowledgment.
entries.what_data_shows: Despite the traffic shift, Wikipedia's active editor count — defined as users making more than five edits per month — has held between 110,000 and 120,000 globally for the past three years according to Wikimedia Statistics. The Foundation launched its own AI working group in 2023 and has piloted AI-assisted citation checking and vandalism detection tools that volunteers report as net productivity gains. A 2024 Stanford Internet Observatory study found no statistically significant increase in AI-generated misinformation successfully persisting on high-traffic Wikipedia articles, suggesting community review mechanisms remain effective.
entries.bigger_picture: The more accurate narrative is that Wikipedia is doing what it has always done: absorbing a technological shift and evolving its processes in response. The community that survived Gamergate, the 2008 financial crisis spam wave, and COVID-19 misinformation floods is not being dismantled by language models — it is deploying them as tools. The real question AI raises for Wikipedia is not survival but mission: if AI can synthesize knowledge, what is the unique value of a human-curated, cited, accountable knowledge commons? The answer — verifiability, editorial accountability, and neutrality policy — is exactly what LLMs structurally cannot provide.

entries.claim: AI deepfakes of celebrities like Mia Goth are spreading uncontrolled on social media — no one is stopping this and it will only get worse
entries.verdict_summary: Non-consensual AI imagery is a real and serious harm, but enforcement infrastructure is expanding rapidly through platform policy, new legislation, and detection tooling — the 'no one is stopping this' framing is already out of date.
entries.what_is_true: Mia Goth's experience is not an edge case — non-consensual AI-generated imagery (NCAII) targeting women, including public figures and private individuals, has surged alongside accessible image generation tools. Instagram's and Meta's content moderation systems have demonstrably failed to catch synthetic celebrity imagery before it goes viral. The psychological harm to targets is real and well-documented. Dismissing these cases because the subject is a celebrity would be wrong: the underlying technology affects everyone, and high-profile cases like this one drive the policy responses that protect ordinary people.
entries.what_data_shows: The claim that 'no one is stopping this' is factually incorrect as of 2024. The U.S. DEFIANCE Act, signed into law in 2024, created federal civil liability for non-consensual intimate AI imagery for the first time. The UK's Online Safety Act explicitly covers AI-generated intimate images. Meta updated its policies in early 2024 to expand the scope of synthetic media it will remove without requiring a court order. Google and Microsoft both added C2PA content provenance metadata requirements to their generative image products in 2024. These are imperfect, early-stage tools — but 'no one is acting' is not supported by the record.
entries.bigger_picture: The trajectory here is important. Every major prior wave of harmful online content — CSAM, revenge porn, coordinated harassment — was met first with platform inaction, then public pressure, then legislation, then enforcement infrastructure. NCAII is moving through that cycle faster than any predecessor, in part because the AI industry's visibility has compressed the policy timeline. The realistic concern is not that nothing will be done, but that enforcement lags the spread of tools by 18 to 36 months. That gap is worth fighting to close — and it is closing.

data_points.l: U.S. DEFIANCE Act signed, creating first federal civil liability for non-consensual intimate AI imagery
content provenance standard now required by Google, Microsoft, and Adobe in generative image products — enables synthetic media detection at scale
major jurisdictions — U.S., UK, and EU — enacted or enforced new NCAII-specific legal protections within a 12-month window ending Q4 2024

entries.claim: AI is completely unregulated — it has fewer rules than milk, and governments are doing nothing to protect us.
entries.verdict_summary: AI is subject to a rapidly expanding global regulatory framework; the 'fewer rules than milk' framing cherry-picks one narrow comparison to obscure substantial existing and incoming law.
entries.what_is_true: The concern has a real kernel. AI regulation is genuinely younger and less standardized than industries like food safety or pharmaceuticals, which have had decades to mature. Microsoft President Brad Smith's 'fewer regulations than milk' line lands because there is no single comprehensive federal AI statute in the United States, and enforcement mechanisms are still being built. For people worried about deepfakes, algorithmic bias, or autonomous weapons, the patchwork feels dangerously thin.
entries.what_data_shows: The regulatory landscape is far more active than the headline implies. The EU AI Act — the world's first comprehensive AI law — entered into force in August 2024 and imposes tiered obligations based on risk level, with fines up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover for the most serious violations. The US already has over 700 state-level AI-related bills introduced across legislatures as of 2024, plus Executive Order 14110 requiring safety evaluations for frontier models above compute thresholds. The UK's AI Safety Institute has conducted structured evaluations of frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind. Simultaneously, OpenAI and Anthropic themselves testified before UK lawmakers requesting regulation — a signal the industry's leading players see binding rules as necessary, not threatening.
entries.bigger_picture: The 'Wild West' framing misses a coordinated international regulatory sprint. The G7 Hiroshima AI Process, the UN's AI Advisory Body report, and bilateral agreements between the US and UK on AI safety testing represent a governance infrastructure being built in real time — faster, arguably, than the internet was ever governed in its first decade. The milk comparison is a useful rhetorical provocation, but the trajectory is clearly toward more structure, not less. The story is one of governance catching up, not governance absent.

entries.claim: AI is heading toward an existential doomsday — even banking regulators are panicking about shifting AI apocalypse timelines.
entries.verdict_summary: Regulators are prudently stress-testing tail risks, but characterizing shifting AI capability timelines as cause for panic misrepresents how risk modeling actually works and ignores the evidence base underlying those timelines.
entries.what_is_true: It is legitimate for financial and systemic regulators to model low-probability, high-impact scenarios — that is their job. The fact that AI capability timelines have surprised even leading researchers is a real phenomenon. Models like GPT-4 and Claude 3 outperformed expectations on standardized benchmarks, and some researchers who previously placed transformative AI decades away have revised their estimates closer. Regulatory bodies ignoring this would itself be a failure. The concern that systemic risk frameworks haven't caught up with AI's pace is not irrational.
entries.what_data_shows: The Gizmodo framing — that shifting predictions 'worry' regulators in an alarming way — obscures that timeline revisions cut both directions and that mainstream AI risk assessments remain probabilistic, not deterministic. The Bank for International Settlements' 2024 working papers on AI treat it primarily as a financial stability and market concentration risk, not an existential one. The UK's AI Safety Institute published structured red-teaming results showing current frontier models do not possess autonomous replication or self-improvement capabilities sufficient to pose systemic danger without human involvement. The much-cited Metaculus community forecast for transformative AI has shifted earlier, yes — but the median estimate still sits years out, and prediction markets reflect high uncertainty, not consensus doom.
entries.bigger_picture: Conflating 'regulators are studying AI risk' with 'doomsday predictions are shifting and causing panic' is a category error that serves fear more than understanding. Banking regulators also model asteroid-strike scenarios and pandemic cascades — doing so is evidence of institutional competence, not alarm. The more important story is that serious institutions are engaging with AI risk with specificity and rigor, building evaluation frameworks and stress tests rather than throwing up their hands. That is exactly what responsible governance looks like, and it deserves to be reported as progress, not panic.

entries.claim: OpenAI claimed a historic AI breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes equations — proof that AI is solving problems humans never could.
entries.verdict_summary: OpenAI's reported Navier-Stokes result was not the landmark proof it was presented as — Scientific American confirmed the claim significantly overstated what the model actually demonstrated.
entries.what_is_true: AI-assisted mathematics is a genuinely exciting and rapidly developing field. Tools like DeepMind's AlphaProof demonstrated real progress on International Mathematical Olympiad problems in 2024, and large language models have shown increasing utility as co-pilots for formal proof verification. The Navier-Stokes equations — which describe fluid dynamics and remain one of the Millennium Prize Problems — would represent one of the most significant mathematical achievements in history if solved. It is reasonable for people to be excited about AI's potential role in advancing pure mathematics.
entries.what_data_shows: According to Scientific American's reporting, OpenAI's blockbuster Navier-Stokes claim was not what it appeared. The result did not constitute a proof of global regularity for the Navier-Stokes equations — the actual Millennium Prize Problem. The work addressed a narrower, specific aspect of the problem, and experts interviewed by Scientific American cautioned that the framing dramatically overstated its scope and significance. This is a pattern worth naming: AI labs have incentives to frame incremental results in maximally impressive terms, and science journalists and peer reviewers serve as a critical check on that tendency — one that functioned correctly in this case.
entries.bigger_picture: This episode is not evidence that AI cannot contribute to mathematics — it is evidence that the scientific community's verification infrastructure works. The overclaim was caught, corrected, and reported. AI-assisted proof tools are genuinely advancing, with DeepMind's FunSearch and AlphaProof producing results that mathematicians have independently validated. The Navier-Stokes episode should raise the bar for how AI mathematical claims are communicated, not generate blanket skepticism about AI's role in science. Accurate representation of incremental progress is more durable — and ultimately more impressive — than overhyped breakthroughs that collapse under scrutiny.

data_points.l: Clay Mathematics Institute prize for actually solving the Navier-Stokes global regularity problem — which remains unsolved
Year DeepMind's AlphaProof achieved independently verified results on International Mathematical Olympiad problems, a legitimate AI math milestone
Scientific American's expert assessment of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes claim after review by mathematicians

entries.claim: AI is going to end the world — doomsday is inevitable and coming soon
entries.verdict_summary: Shifting AI doomsday timelines and Atlantic-style existential panic reflect genuine uncertainty, but conflate speculative risk with near-term reality in ways the evidence does not support.
entries.what_is_true: The concern is not frivolous. Serious researchers at places like DeepMind, Anthropic, and the Centre for Human-Compatible AI have published peer-reviewed work on long-term risks from misaligned AI systems. The fact that AI doomsday predictions keep shifting — as reported by banking regulators tracking AI risk narratives — does reflect real expert disagreement about trajectory and timelines. Dismissing these conversations entirely would be intellectually dishonest.
entries.what_data_shows: What the data does not show is imminent civilizational collapse. A 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers published in AI Magazine found the median estimate for transformative AI was 2047, with enormous variance — meaning there is no consensus on timeline, let alone outcome. The AI safety field itself is growing: Anthropic, DeepMind's safety team, and OpenAI's preparedness team collectively employ hundreds of researchers specifically tasked with preventing catastrophic outcomes. Regulatory frameworks are accelerating — the EU AI Act is now enforceable, the UK AI Safety Institute is operational, and OpenAI and Anthropic voluntarily appeared before British lawmakers to request oversight. These are not the conditions of a field racing recklessly toward doom.
entries.bigger_picture: The 'end of the world' framing crowds out the more tractable, immediate questions about AI governance, bias, and labor displacement — problems that are real, measurable, and solvable. Existential panic also historically correlates with worse policy outcomes: fear-driven regulation tends to be blunt and counterproductive. The AI Safety community's own leading voices, including Yoshua Bengio, advocate for structured international cooperation — not fatalism. The trajectory here is more guardrails, more transparency, and more institutional accountability, not less.

entries.claim: OpenAI's AI solved a 100-year-old math problem — proof that AI is already smarter than human experts
entries.verdict_summary: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes claim was significantly walked back upon scrutiny — it demonstrates AI's real but narrowly-scoped mathematical utility, not general superhuman reasoning.
entries.what_is_true: The excitement is understandable. If AI systems could genuinely resolve the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem — one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems with a $1 million prize — it would represent one of the most significant mathematical breakthroughs in a century. The Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid dynamics and remain unsolved in three dimensions. AI systems like AlphaProof have demonstrated genuine, peer-validated progress on competition-level mathematics, so the optimism behind these headlines is not baseless.
entries.what_data_shows: Scientific American reported directly that OpenAI's blockbuster Navier-Stokes proof 'isn't what we thought it was.' Independent mathematicians who reviewed the claim found it addressed a narrower, already-known result rather than the full Millennium Problem. This is consistent with a documented pattern: AI systems excel at recombining known mathematical structures and verifying formal proofs, but have not demonstrated the capacity to produce fundamentally novel mathematical insight at the level required for unsolved Millennium Problems. AlphaProof's verified achievements — gold-medal-level performance on six 2024 IMO problems — are impressive but operate within structured, bounded problem spaces.
entries.bigger_picture: The real story here is actually more interesting than the hype. AI is becoming a genuine force-multiplier for human mathematicians — accelerating proof verification, exploring solution spaces, and handling computational grunt work that previously took years. Fields Medal winner Terence Tao has publicly described using AI tools as 'a collaborator.' That is a transformative and positive development. But credibility in AI reporting requires distinguishing between 'AI assists expert mathematicians' and 'AI surpasses all human mathematical ability' — and right now, the evidence clearly supports only the former.

data_points.l: Millennium Prize for solving Navier-Stokes — still unclaimed after OpenAI's announcement was scrutinized
IMO 2024 problems solved at gold-medal level by AlphaProof — a genuine, verified benchmark
Millennium Prize Problems formally verified as solved by any AI system to date
